Inventoria · food search, end to end

How Inventoria finds a food

You type beef. Something decides which of USDA's 7,974 published records you are allowed to see, which of the survivors your word reaches, and which of those goes first. This is all three — and then every one of the 5,537 foods the first decision discarded, with the rule and the words that removed it.

01 · The short answer

Three narrowings, two of them invisible

Search is not one filter. It is a membership decision taken at build time, a retrieval decision taken on your keystroke, and an ordering decision taken on what survived both. Most of the work — 69% of everything USDA published — happened before you opened the app.

The whole pipeline is local. There is no search server, no API key and no network call: a committed JSON file ships with the app, is parsed in about 14 ms, and every keystroke ranks all 2,437 rows in memory. Search works on a plane.

Bars are to scale against the 7,974 records USDA publishes. The last row is the honest one: the most-logged beef there is sits past the 50-row page, so typing beef cannot reach it at all.

02 · Try it

Search the real corpus

This is not a demo. The 2,437-row corpus below and the code ranking it are the ones the app ships — usda-corpus.ts bundled for the browser, the same searchIndexRows a keystroke calls. Type and you get exactly what the app would answer, cap and all.

Queries this page argues about:

 

Each row shows the key vector that placed it, read left to right exactly as compareRelevance reads it — the first column where two rows differ is the one that decided them. tier is the six rungs; pos is how far into the name your words landed; sib, raw and desig are read off the row rather than the name.

Two annotations can appear under a row, and they are different things. A name in brackets — Eggplant (aubergine) — is another name FOR the food, and the app shows it too, in the name itself, so the word you typed follows the food into your log. A line reading reached through USDA’s discarded name is not a name for the food at all: it is the losing half of a twin merge, or a filing a rename replaced, and it explains why a row surfaced when the words you typed appear nowhere on it. This page shows that line and the app does not — the app has to answer, this page has to explain — and it is kept out of the name on both, because Eggs, Grade A, Large, egg whole is USDA’s paperwork and not what anybody calls an egg.

03 · Sources

Four places a food can come from

Only one of them is a text search. Knowing which is which explains most of what looks inconsistent about the screen.

SourceReached bySizeWhat it is for
USDA reference foodstyping a word2,437Base ingredients — the things you cook with. The only text-searchable table.
Open Food Factsscanning a barcode—Packaged products. Deliberately not text-searchable. No packet, no product.
Curated stand-instyping a word2Hand-captured products for base foods USDA lacks: cacao nibs, double cream. Capped at 8.
Your own ledgerRecent list—Anything you logged before. Sorted by time, not ranked.

When you type, the curated table and the USDA corpus are searched with the same phrases, and the results are stitched in a fixed order: exact curated hits first, then every USDA row, then partial curated hits. So typing cacao nibs leads with the stand-in, while a broad cocoa never displaces USDA's cocoa powder.

Why products are not text-searchable

Open Food Facts is crowd-sourced and enormous, and a text search over it would bury a plain onion under forty branded onion products. Barcode-only is a deliberate refusal, not a missing feature — and it is a known cost: if the packet is already in the bin, the product is unreachable.

04 · The spine

Membership is decided once; retrieval is decided every keystroke

This split is the single most useful thing to hold onto. Two completely different sets of rules run at two completely different times, and confusing them is how almost every question about search goes wrong.

MembershipRetrieval & order
WhenOnce, when the artifact is generatedEvery keystroke, in your browser
QuestionIs this a food a person logs?Does this word reach it, and how well?
Instrument19 drop rules + 4 name rosters6 tier rungs + 11 ordering keys
FailureA food is gone and nothing says soA food is there but buried
Recoverable?No — you cannot scroll to a row that never shippedYes — by scrolling

That asymmetry is why the rules are lopsided, and why the rest of this page is mostly about the left-hand column. A wrong order costs a scroll. A wrong drop costs the food, silently, with nothing on screen to notice.

05 · The review surface

What was discarded

5,537 of USDA's 7,974 records never reach the app — 69% of everything published. A dropped record is simply absent from the shipped index, with nothing anywhere saying which rule took it. This section is the reconstruction: every one of them, the rule that removed it, and the terms that rule fired on.

The cause is found by ablation, not by reading a table. The filters' word lists are deliberately private, so a page that copied them would be a second copy of two hundred lines of editorial judgement, drifting quietly. Instead each record is asked of the real rule with terms removed one at a time, and what is reported is the minimal sufficient removal set: the smallest set of terms you could delete and have the rule go quiet. It survives a rewrite of the rules.

Rules are asked in this order, and a record is attributed to the first one to fire — the one that actually removed it. So a family's count is the records that reached it, not the records that match it.

2,136removed by a single word in the name
969removed by USDA's own filing alone — the name says nothing
2,281needed several terms acting together
151have no word to point at — the rule reads the corpus or the panel
The largest single cause is not a word

It is USDA's own foodCategory, which alone removes 969 records — files them under Baked Products or Fast Foods and their descriptions say nothing about preparation at all. Whether to trust another organisation's filing that far is a real question, and it is the one this page most wants a reviewer to look at.

07 · By category

The filters cut on a cliff, not a gradient

Sorted by how many records USDA published in each of its own categories. The striking thing is the shape: 8 categories lost every single record (1,640 rows between them) while 1 kept over 90%. Very few sit in between.

That is not a rule anybody wrote. It is what happens when “is this an ingredient?” meets a filing system built around meals — and it means the categories that vanished are worth an eyeball, because nothing inside them was individually judged.

08 · Every one of them

Review all 5,537 discarded foods

Filter by rule, by USDA category, or by typing. Each row shows the food as USDA named it, the rule that removed it, and — where there is one — the terms the rule fired on, which are highlighted in the name.

 

09 · Keystroke, part one

What your word reaches

USDA names a food Food, qualifier, qualifier. Everything below leans on that: the head phrase before the first comma is the food's identity, and everything after it is description. Retrieval scores how much of a food's own name your query accounts for, on six rungs.

The tier ladder — strongest first, as the list reads

50The head phrase is your query.“grape” → Grapes, muscadine
40A typed word is a head word.“grape” → Grape leaves
30The head completes what you are still typing.“pot” → Potatoes, flesh and skin
20A whole typed word, but only in a qualifier.“grape” → Tomatoes, grape
10A typed word merely prefixes some word, anywhere.“pot” → Jute, potherb
0No match at all. The row never enters the result set.the row is not in the result set

Rung 40 sits above rung 30 deliberately: for “grape”, grape leaves are a grape and a grapefruit is not.

The stray-mention rule

USDA writes an ingredient where a qualifier goes, so Cheese, mozzarella, whole milk matches the word milk perfectly well. So a row whose every typed word landed past the food's own name is dropped — but only where some other row answered on a strictly higher rung. That second condition is what makes it structural rather than a judgement call: the leading row can never be dropped, and a query no name answers leaves the bar at 0 so nothing is cut.

When your word reaches nothing at all

Only then — and the gate is absolute — a vocabulary map runs. It holds 430 phrases derived from Open Food Facts' ingredient taxonomy plus 7 hand-written British entries OFF does not carry: caster sugar, gammon, mange tout, natural yoghurt, plain flour, porridge oats, soymilk.

Why the gate is absolute

Because the expansion only runs when the literal search returned zero rows, an expansion can never reorder, displace or truncate a result you would have got anyway. The no-regression property is structural rather than a promise — which is also why the ranking has no key, tier or clause for the vocabulary at all.

10 · Keystroke, part two

Twelve keys, read in order, never summed

Every retrieved row gets 12 numbers. They are compared strictly in sequence — a tie on the first is broken by the second — so an earlier key is never traded against a later one. A row scores as the best of all its names, including the 73 rows carrying aliases a merge discarded.

The cascade, best-first · right column = leads that move if the key is removed

1tierThe six rungs above — how much of the food's own name you accounted for.76
2recentHow recently you logged this exact food on this device (#165). 0 for a food you never have.0
3frequentHow often you have logged it, decayed so that forty times last year weighs less than five times this week.0
4canonicalA hand-written roster, two entries long: where rows tie all the way down, name the one the query actually means.6
5rawPrefer a raw food to a prepared one.72
6headHow completely your query fills the head phrase.20
7accountedIs every word of the name answered? A boolean, because counting leftovers prefers “Chicken, ground” to a whole chicken.8
8positionHow far into the name your words landed, summed. USDA orders qualifiers by importance, so depth says how much the food is that thing.189
9plainSiblingDemote a row when a plainer version of it exists elsewhere in the corpus.59
10plainDemote an imitation, a substitute, a reduced-fat form or a cooked one.30
11wholeness2 for a whole animal averaged over its cuts, 0 for a fat trimmed off it, 1 for everything between.8
12designatedWhere two rows tie on everything else, prefer the one not published for a specific population.10

Counts are read from 192-key-census.json, measured by ablation over a 2,634-query sweep built from every head phrase and head word in the corpus. Six of these read the row rather than its name — the two frecency keys, canonical, raw, plainSibling and designated — which is why a careless measuring harness loses them silently. recent and frequent measure zero here because this corpus has no ledger behind it; on a device that has logged nothing they tie on every row, and what is left is the eleven-key ranking everyone who has logged nothing gets.

Why each of them exists

Not one was designed up front. Each arrived because a specific query led with a specific wrong row:

  • position — olive oil led with Oil, corn, peanut, and olive, a blend, for a query naming a single oil.
  • accounted — soybean oil led with Oil, soybean lecithin, an emulsifier, because two rows agreed on every key and the lower id won.
  • wholeness — australian beef led with external fat, and demoting that promoted seam fat at 562 kcal.
  • plainSibling — fifteen red and thirteen white varietal wines sitting above the wine they are varieties of.

11 · Display

What actually reaches the screen

The ranked list is cut to 50 rows, and that is the last narrowing. Nothing below 50 is reachable by any means except typing a different word.

A ranked list · searching “grape”

Grapes, muscadine
Grapes, american type (slip skin)
Grapes, red or green (European type, such as Thompson seedless)
Grapes, red, seedless
Grapes, green, seedless

The real top five, ranked by the app's own comparator at generation time. The winner inverts — ink on paper. The runners-up carry a stepping left edge that thins over three rows and then stops, which is where the list stops making a claim worth reading.

A chronology gets no rank mark at all. Your Recent list is sorted by time; its newest entry won nothing, and painting a crown over it would be a claim about order the list does not make. That was a real shipped defect, and the rule now reads: a presentation meaning “this one won” may not appear over a list that has not ranked anything.

13 · Honesty

How good is it, really

Before any of this was changed, a bar was written down and committed — 44 hand-judged queries, each with the exact record a diarist means, keyed by USDA id so a rename cannot fake a pass.

ConditionAsksToday
C1Is the row you meant in the top three?24 / 44
C2Does the query answer with 25 rows or fewer?27 / 44

So search fails its own bar on roughly half of ordinary one-word queries. Four gold rows are off the screen entirely — three past the 50-row page cap and one not retrieved at all. C2 was chosen over a cleverer proposal for one reason: result-set size is the one number ranking cannot move.

14 · Trade-offs

Every choice, and what it costs

ChoiceBuysCosts
Bundle the corpus; no APINo key, no quota, offline search, 14 ms parseA 1.7 MB file in the app; refreshing it is a code change
USDA over other national tables95% of rows carry a household portion; deep nutrient panelsThe worst table on duplication: 8.28 rows per head against CIQUAL's 2.00
Barcode-only productsA typed word reaches ingredients, never forty branded onionsNo packet, no product
Drop rather than rank packaged foods5,537 rows of noise never reach a keystrokeA food dropped in error is unreachable and silent
Trust USDA's own filing969 dishes removed without hand-judging each8 categories vanish whole, unexamined
Keep cooked rows, demote themA logged bowl of rice is not costed at dry-rice energy — ~360 kcal against ~13041% of the corpus names a cooking method, so lists are long
Vocabulary only on zero resultsAn expansion can never damage a result you already hadraw aubergine gets no help, because the map is phrase-keyed
Ordinal keys, never summedOne key can never be outvoted by two weaker onesDeep ties are broken by USDA id — effectively arbitrary
50-row pageA bounded list, a bounded render11 of 45 queries hit it, and three correct answers sit past it
The standing risk

90% of what ships is SR Legacy, which USDA stopped maintaining in 2018. Thirteen national composition tables were surveyed for a replacement; none is more current and better on duplication and carries household portions.

15 · What the rule cost

One row per ingredient, and the fourteen foods it took

The corpus used to carry every record USDA published about a food, including the ones it had cooked first. Typing beef returned rows that were the same sentence permuted over trim, grade, separation and cooking. That list was not mis-sorted — it was one food written out thirty times, and no ordering of thirty copies produces fewer than thirty.

The rule the corpus now follows

A corpus row is a food as bought. Cooking happens after the purchase, so a cooked record is not an ingredient and does not ship. Drying, curing and smoking happen before it, so dried apricots and smoked salmon are foods and do.

The line between them is a shop: if you could scoop it out of a bin and carry it home in a paper bag with no label on it, it is an ingredient. That is why roasted peanuts and toasted sunflower seeds stay and parboiled rice does not.

1,750 records left on that rule alone. A name then loses the words that only existed to deny an alternative — every spelling of the uncooked state, an enrichment word whose counterpart no longer ships, and a comparative like regular that nothing contests any more:

Rice, white, long-grain, regular, raw, enriched
  -> Rice, white, long-grain

What it cost, stated rather than buried

Fourteen foods left the corpus entirely, because the only record USDA published of each was a cooked one. There is no version of this rule that keeps them: a rule reading one row at a time cannot tell a duplicate from the only record there is.

GoneWhy
mutton, turkey breast, turkey thigh, doveUSDA publishes them roasted and no other way
escarole, stinging nettles, malabar spinach, tree fernpublished boiled
buckwheat groats, pinon nuts, winged beanpublished cooked or roasted
salmon nuggets, guava sauce, beef compositepublished cooked

A British reader loses one more thing worth naming: jacket potato no longer answers. A jacket potato is a baked potato, so there is no uncooked row for the word to reach. A raw potato is still in the corpus and still answers potato.

What it bought

2,437rows, down from 4,238 — and 498 foods, down from 512
25%of rows unreachable by typing the corpus's own vocabulary, down from 41%
412rows answer beef
0leads the simplicity ranking key still moves

That last figure is the one nobody was looking for. Removing the cooked rows retired a ranking key. simplicity now moves no lead at all and breaks nothing when deleted, and raw has fallen from 63 moved leads to 72 — it was reading a word no name carries any more. An earlier census went looking for exactly this and found nothing redundant; what it was testing was a rule that merged duplicate rows, and merging leaves every distinction standing. Removing them does not.

It also repaired five cases a hand-adjudication had recorded as wrong. spinach used to lead with Spinach, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt; millet, teff, tempeh and rice noodles led with their cooked rows too. All five leads were wrong because a cooked row was answering, and all five rows are gone.

16 · Questions

Questions this usually raises

How do I check whether a food I expected is missing?

Type it into the browser in section 7. If it is there, the row tells you which rule removed it and which words that rule fired on. If it is not there and it is not in the app either, it is a food USDA never published — the census covers every record in both archives, and its survivor count is checked against the shipped index on every regeneration, so it cannot quietly miss a record.

Why did egg used to lead with a duck egg?

It no longer does, and the way it stopped is worth reading, because the obvious fix was not the one that worked.

USDA names four birds — Egg, duck, whole, fresh, goose, quail, turkey — and then files a hen's egg under its retail grade, as Eggs, Grade A, Large, egg whole. So the one egg nearly everybody means was the only one whose name never said which bird laid it, and it lost on two keys at once: the plural Eggs filled the head phrase less completely than Egg, and USDA never wrote raw on a graded egg, so a box of fresh eggs scored 0 on a key the duck scored 1 on.

Renaming it was necessary and not sufficient. Shipped as Egg, chicken, whole, fresh the row matches its four siblings exactly — and that is the problem: same tier, same head, same everything the keys can read. All five tied to the bottom of the comparator, where the sort fell through to corpus order and the duck's lower record number won. Nothing about that was a judgement.

So the tie is broken by canonical, a hand-written roster with two entries in it, sitting just below the two frecency keys. Below them on purpose: if you log duck eggs, duck leads. A roster rather than a rule because there is no rule to write — the names differ only in the bird, and which bird is the default is knowledge about shoppers, not about food composition. It moves 6 leads across the whole sweep, and it can never remove a row: every egg is still there, in the order the next key down would have put them.

Why did cow milk used to find nothing?

The same shape as the eggs, one step worse. USDA names three animals under the head phrase Milk — Milk, sheep, fluid, Milk, goat, fluid, Milk, indian buffalo, fluid — and then files cow's milk by its fat content. So the milk almost every search means was the only one that never said which animal it came from, milk led with sheep, and cow milk returned zero rows.

The four fluid milks now say it: Milk, cow, whole, 3.7% milkfat and its 2%, 1% and skimmed siblings. Evaporated milk and buttermilk are cow's milk too and are deliberately left alone — nobody says “cow buttermilk”, and the word only earns its place where an animal is genuinely in question.

This is a rename, not a species rule. A ranking key that read animal words out of descriptions was designed, measured and refused, and that refusal stands: there is no roster of animals anywhere in the search, and goat, sheep and buffalo milk hold every position they had relative to each other. What changed is that the corpus now states the species in the data, in the same place USDA already states it for the other three — which is also the only thing that could fix the retrieval, since no ordering key can return a row that the words never reach.

Why is there no “popularity” ranking?

Nothing leaves the device, so there is no shared usage data to rank on. What ranking there is comes from two places, and both obey the same standing principle — prevalence may rank a food and may never drop one.

The first is your own log: recent and frequent are computed on this device from what you have actually eaten, and they sit above every other ordering key. The second is canonical, two hand-written entries, which fire only on rows that tie in every earlier key. Ranking by assumed prevalence as a drop rule was considered and refused outright.

Is “the rule fired on this word” the same as “this word is in a denylist”?

No, and the difference matters. The census never reads the rules' word lists — they are private, and copying them would be a second copy of the judgement. It removes terms from the record until the real rule goes quiet, and reports the smallest set that keeps it quiet. So a term shown here is load-bearing for this verdict, which is a stronger and more useful claim than naming a table entry, and it survives a rewrite of the table.

Some rows show no terms at all. Why?

Because those rules do not read the name. superseded is a hand-written id list, no_energy reads the nutrient panel, the three variant rules ask what a row's head-phrase siblings look like, and the name-collision rules ask what other rows are called. There is no word to point at, and the census says so rather than inventing one.

Do I lose past logs when a row leaves the corpus?

No. A logged food carries its own nutrient panel into the append-only ledger, and nothing re-reads the search index for a past log. Dropping rows cannot damage history — which is why membership changes are safe to make and ordering changes are the fiddly ones.

Why are raw and cooked the same food, but whole and skimmed milk are not?

The meal-log test. You buy beef and cook it, so cooking happened after the purchase and collapses. You buy 2% milk as 2% milk, so fat content is true at purchase and distinguishes. Nutritional distance is explicitly not the test — a threshold on calorie movement was built and refuted, because cooking moves a chicken breast 13% and trim moves beef 12%, one point apart.

If a collapse throws away a measured difference, which number do I get?

One real USDA record's panel, whole — never a mean, because a mean is a number USDA never measured and no row can be pointed at to explain it. The survivor is chosen by fullest nutrient panel, then lowest id.

What happens when USDA has no good record?

The group ships its fullest-panel row under that row's whole, unstripped name. So Quinoa, cooked ships saying exactly that, rather than being renamed to Quinoa and quietly claiming to be the dry grain. A name may never claim less than its panel measures.

How do I regenerate this page?

pnpm usda:drop-census rebuilds the census from the archives in .usda-backup, then pnpm docs:food-search rebuilds this page from the census and the shipped index. pnpm docs:food-search --check fails if the committed page is out of date, and runs in pnpm check.
